name: Meet Xara
tagline: A branded AI assistant you talk to instead of doing the work yourself.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This sits in the most clonable product category of the decade: a friendly front end over somebody else's language model. The chat loop, the persona, the memory of past conversations, the little tool calls, all of that is a weekend of work for an agent that knows what it is doing. What does not come for free is everything around the loop: the integrations into the places you actually live, the phone or messaging channel, and the hundred small reliability fixes that stop an assistant from confidently inventing things. We have not verified the exact feature set here, so treat this as a verdict on the shape of the product rather than on its deepest corner. If your use is personal and your tolerance for rough edges is normal, a local build gets you most of the way.
coreLoopDIY: A local chat assistant with a fixed persona, persistent conversation memory in SQLite, and a few tool calls it can actually run.
requirements: An API key for a hosted LLM, or a local model if you have the hardware
Node 20 and a place to run it, localhost is fine
A messaging bot token if you want it anywhere but the browser
whatYouLose: Mobile and messaging channels, unless you wire up a bot yourself
Any integrations into calendar, email, or business tools that the paid product ships
Prompt and guardrail tuning that someone else already paid for in support tickets
Multilingual polish, including whatever the Spanish experience does well
Someone to blame when the assistant hallucinates at an inconvenient moment
moatNotes: The model is rented by everyone. What differentiates is the plumbing on both ends and how rarely it embarrasses you.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for assistants because they do not want to maintain one. A self-hosted clone means you own the prompt drift, the API bills, the broken tool calls, and the day the model provider changes behavior without telling you. A paid product absorbs that and shows up already connected to the systems you use, in the language you use, with a support channel. If the assistant is doing real work rather than being a toy, the subscription is usually cheaper than the attention it takes to keep a homemade one honest.
notes: The chat box is the easy part; the integrations are the product.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user AI assistant web app. No accounts, no cloud backend, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for all persistence, file at ./data/assistant.db
- An OpenAI-compatible chat completions client, base URL and API key read from .env (LLM_API_KEY, LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_MODEL)
- Zod for validating tool call arguments

What to build:
1. A single chat page: message list, streaming assistant responses, Markdown rendering, a sidebar listing past conversations.
2. Conversations and messages persisted in SQLite. Resume any conversation, rename it, delete it.
3. A persona layer: a system prompt stored in a config file I can edit, plus a "facts about me" table the assistant can read on every turn and append to when I tell it something worth remembering. Show those facts on a /memory page where I can edit or delete rows.
4. Tool calling with exactly three tools, no more: get_current_time, search_notes (full text search over a ./notes folder of Markdown files), and save_fact (writes to the facts table). Validate args with Zod, return errors as tool results instead of crashing.
5. Token and cost accounting: store prompt and completion tokens per message, show a running total per conversation.
6. Language toggle: the UI strings and the system prompt switch between English and Spanish from a single messages file.

Explicitly out of scope: voice input, WhatsApp or Telegram, calendar or email integrations, multi-user auth, vector databases, any hosted service beyond the LLM endpoint.

Deliverables: working app via npm install and npm run dev, .env.example with the three keys, a seed script that creates the DB, and a README that is under 40 lines and tells me how to change the persona.
Write real code, not stubs. If a design decision is ambiguous, pick one and note it in the README.
